passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and I sit next to Damini in Class 5. On Career Day, Miss asked us to draw what we'd be. Damini drew a doctor with a stethoscope before Miss had even finished speaking. "My grandfather was a doctor, my mother is a doctor, so I'm going to be a doctor," she told the whole row, chin up. When Miss asked, "What do you like about it?" Damini said, "Everyone in my family is one," and looked surprised that there could be another kind of answer. At lunch she drew rockets on her tiffin napkin, like she always does. I don't know what's in her head. But she said the word doctor the way you say your own name.

qa.a: Miss could ask Damini about the rockets too, opening space to explore her own interests while still respecting the doctor plan.

qa.a: Lalremsiami notices Damini says it like her own name, as something given and certain, while admitting not knowing what Damini really thinks.

passage: Vaibhav Dadu smiled at his granddaughter. "You want to know why I became a teacher and not a doctor, Yamini? When I was nine, in our house in Nagpur, everybody asked me, 'What will you become?' I would stand straight and say, 'Doctor!' My father smiled, my aunts pinched my cheek. It felt wonderful. Nobody argued, so I never wondered. It was like wearing my elder cousin's school blazer: it came to me already made. Then at twelve, a neighbour asked me to explain the stars to her little ones on the terrace, and I talked for an hour. That night I understood that 'doctor' was a word I carried, not a thing I had chosen. It took me years to say so aloud."

The lights went out at seven, and Jatin's essay, "My Aim in Life", was due tomorrow. By the candle on the dining table he wrote in his best letters: I will be an engineer like Papa and Ramesh Chacha.
"Good boy," said Ramesh Chacha, holding the candle closer. Jatin wrote the same sentence again at the end and underlined it twice. Wax dripped onto the page, and he scraped it off carefully.
From the sofa, his little cousin Pinky asked, "What does an engineer do all day?"
Jatin thought. "Big things. Bridges. Papa knows." He bent over his page again, proud and calm. Nobody at home had ever asked him what else he might like, and in the dark it felt good to be so sure.

qa.a: The title was My Aim in Life.

qa.a: They could ask what he likes about bridges, or what else he enjoys, so the goal becomes something he looks into rather than just repeats.

qa.a: He might notice that Jatin knows little about the job he claims, and wonder whether the aim is truly Jatin's own.

At the Children's Day programme in the party hall of their Kochi apartment block, Elizabeth Aunty held the microphone out to each child. "And what will you become?"
Salma, eleven, didn't even pause. "A chartered accountant, like my Umma and Uppa. I'll join their office." Several aunties clapped, and her Uppa, in the second row, raised his tea cup.
"What do you like best about accounts, Salma?"
Salma blinked. "It's... a very good job. Everybody in our family says so." She said it louder, and the clapping came again.
Back in her seat she swung her legs, pleased. The question about liking it had slid off her like rain off the balcony glass. Nobody asked it twice.

qa.a: A chartered accountant, like her Umma and Uppa.

qa.a: She feels pleased and sure of her answer, yet her blink suggests she had never thought about what she actually likes in the job.

qa.q: What could Salma's parents do later that evening to help her explore without taking away her pride?
qa.a: They could ask what she enjoys at school and mention other paths too, so accounts becomes a choice she tests, not only one she repeats.

qa.a: That Salma could name the job but not one reason she likes it, a sign the goal is borrowed rather than explored.

Chandrika, beti, you told the whole wedding you'll be an engineer like your father. Very good. Let me tell you something about me at your age.
When I was ten, in Jodhpur, every uncle asked me, "What will you become?" And I always said, proudly, "Engineer!" My father and his brother were engineers. It felt like the answer to a question on a test.
I never once asked myself if I wanted it.
Then, at fifteen, my school had a drama competition. I played a king. And standing on that stage, with everyone listening, I felt something I'd never felt with maths.
I did become an engineer, beti. I'm Kamal, and I was a good one. But I always wondered what would have happened if someone had asked me what I loved.

qa.a: Kamal felt proud and certain, as if giving the right answer on a test.

qa.a: Playing a king in the drama competition was the turning point, because it revealed a feeling Kamal had never explored behind the handed-down role.

qa.q: How might Kamal's father have seen young Kamal's answer?
qa.a: Kamal's father probably felt proud and pleased that Kamal wanted to follow him.

The wedding hall was so loud that Deepak, ten, had to shout, and the relatives kept asking the same question between rounds of sweets.
"What will you be, beta?"
"IAS officer!" Deepak said each time, proudly. Like his uncle. Like his mother had wanted.
Everyone nodded. "Very good boy."
Behind the stage, his cousin Naveen, fourteen, was hiding from the dancing. "Why IAS?" he asked.
Deepak shrugged. "Everyone says it."
"But what do they do all day?"
Deepak opened his mouth. He didn't know. He only knew that when he said it, everyone smiled and nobody asked anything else. It felt safe.
"Doesn't matter," he said. "I'll be one."
But on the way home, looking out of the car window, he kept wondering what an IAS officer actually did.

When I was ten, I told everyone I'd be a chartered accountant. I'm Noor, and my Abbu and both uncles are accountants. It sounded important, and every time I said it, the grown-ups smiled.
In Class 5, our teacher, Thomas Sir, asked us to write about our dream jobs and why. I wrote "CA" and then stopped. I didn't know why. I'd never asked myself.
I copied what Abbu says: "It's a respectable profession." Thomas Sir wrote in the margin: "What do YOU enjoy?"
I stared at that for a long time. I liked making clay animals. I liked explaining things to my little brother.
I still said CA at the next family dinner. It felt safe. But the question stayed.

Diwali night.
Dear diary, so many relatives came today! Everyone asked the same question: 'Vikas, what will you become?' And I said ENGINEER every time, loud, like Papa taught me. Papa is an engineer, Dada was an engineer, and Mridul Bhaiya is doing engineering in Pune. Bua pinched my cheek and said, 'Our family's fourth engineer!' Everyone clapped. I felt so proud, like I had already passed. Then on the terrace, while we lit phuljhadis, Mridul Bhaiya asked me quietly, 'What do you actually like doing?' I said engineering. He said, 'No, like, what makes you forget time?' I said drawing comics. He laughed and said engineers can draw too. I don't know why that question made my tummy feel funny. Anyway, I'm going to be an engineer.
Vikas
